meta.title: Marketing
meta.range: HSC topic · 25% of course time · developing and implementing successful marketing strategies

boxes.label: Examinable
boxes.bodyHtml: Role of marketing, types of markets, influences on marketing (customer choice, consumer laws, ethics), the marketing process (situational analysis, market research, objectives, target markets, strategy, implementation/monitoring/controlling) and marketing strategies (segmentation/differentiation/positioning, the 4 Ps, global marketing) — all Learn To and Learn About dot points.

boxes.label: Format reminder
boxes.bodyHtml: The HSC Business Studies exam draws on all four topics: Section I is 20 multiple-choice questions, Section II is short-answer questions spanning all topics, Section III is a business-report extended response, and Section IV offers a choice of extended-response questions by topic.

summary.note: Organised by the syllabus's own headings for this topic.

groups.title: Role of marketing
points: Marketing is a total system of interacting activities designed to plan, price, promote and distribute products to existing and potential customers — advertising is only one part of marketing, not the whole of it.
The marketing mix (4 Ps) is Product, Price, Promotion and Place; the strategic role of marketing is to support profit maximisation by increasing sales, market share and brand awareness.
Non-profit organisations market to inform and raise awareness rather than to sell — objectives are social rather than financial, e.g. Oxfam, quit-smoking campaigns.

The three historical approaches to marketing are the production approach (1820s–1920s, produce as much as possible cheaply, e.g. Ford's Model T), the selling approach (1920s–1960s, emphasise selling as supply began to exceed demand) and the modern marketing approach (1960s–present, research what customers want, then satisfy it) — the marketing concept is customer-orientated and integrated into the whole business plan.

Interdependence: marketing relies on operations to produce goods to the right standard, on finance for budgets and pricing information, and on HR to recruit and train the right staff — while marketing in turn shapes what each of those functions needs to do. Real example: the ACCC took Qantas to court in 2023 for continuing to advertise and sell tickets on flights it had already decided to cancel — marketing had continued selling a service operations had already withdrawn, the exact failure the interdependence dot point warns against.

Types of markets include resource (primary production, e.g. mining), industrial (business-to-business), intermediate (wholesalers/retailers who resell), consumer (individuals who use what they buy), mass (one product to all buyers, e.g. basic utilities) and niche (a small, specific segment with unique needs, e.g. plus-size clothing).

groups.title: Influences on marketing
points: Customer choice is shaped by psychological factors (perceptions, motives, attitudes, personality, learning/brand loyalty), sociocultural factors (social class, culture, family role, peer group), economic conditions (boom vs recession changing spending willingness) and government policy and regulation. Real example: the ACCC's supermarkets inquiry (final report, February 2025) found Woolworths (about 38% of national grocery sales) and Coles (about 29%) operate in an oligopolistic market structure with limited incentive to compete vigorously on price, and made 20 recommendations including price transparency and disclosure when product sizes shrink ('shrinkflation').

Key consumer laws include the Australian Consumer Law (2011) (a single national law giving all consumers the same rights) and the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (protects consumers against unfair practices and protects competition), both enforced by the ACCC and ASIC — breaches can bring infringement notices, public warning notices or court penalties (up to $1.1m for companies).

Deceptive and misleading advertising (e.g. greenwashing, bait and switch) is specifically regulated. Real example: on 14 May 2026 the Federal Court found Coles had breached the Australian Consumer Law over its 'Down Down' promotions — of 14 promotional tickets examined, 13 were misleading because prices had been temporarily raised (e.g. Karicare formula held at $18 for 794 days, lifted to $24 for 23 days, then advertised as 'Down Down' at $21 — still $3 above the original price) before being advertised as discounted.

Price discrimination (illegal unless justified by cost differences or matching a competitor in good faith), implied conditions (now consumer guarantees under the ACL) and warranties are also specifically regulated.

Ethical concerns in marketing include truth, accuracy and good taste in advertising (avoiding concealed facts, exaggerated claims, stereotypes), promoting products that may damage health (e.g. junk food advertising restrictions), engaging in fair competition (avoiding cartel conduct, misuse of market power, predatory pricing) and sugging (selling disguised as market research). Real example: Qantas' 'ghost flights' conduct — advertising and selling tickets on flights already decided to be cancelled, and not promptly notifying more than 10,000 existing ticketholders, between 21 May 2021 and 26 August 2023 — resulted in a $100 million penalty and roughly $20 million in payments to 86,597 affected consumers, one of the clearest available examples of the direct financial cost of unethical, misleading promotion.

groups.title: The marketing process
points: The marketing process (SMEDI): Situational analysis (SWOT and product life cycle), Market research, Establishing objectives, Identifying target markets, Developing strategies, and Implementation, monitoring and controlling.
A SWOT analysis examines internal Strengths and Weaknesses (controllable) and external Opportunities and Threats (must be responded to, not controlled).

The product life cycle has four stages — introduction (low sales, high cost, low price to gain a foothold), growth (rising sales, differentiation from new competitors), maturity (peak demand, saturated market, focus on retaining customers) and decline (falling sales, reduced promotion, possible product deletion).

Market research estimates demand, analyses competition, defines the target market and uncovers market opportunities, using primary data (observation, survey, experiment methods — collected specifically for the problem) and secondary data (already collected by others, e.g. ABS census data — cheaper but less specific).

Market objectives should be specific and measurable (e.g. 'increase market share by 5% over 12 months'); common objectives are increasing sales, increasing market share, maximising customer service and expanding the product range.

A target market is the group of present and potential customers a business sells to — approaches include mass marketing (one product for everyone), market segmentation (dividing the market by shared characteristics) and niche marketing (a narrow, specific segment).
Consumer markets are segmented by demographic (age, income, etc.), geographic (location), psychographic (lifestyle, personality) and behavioural (relationship to the product) variables.

Implementation, monitoring and controlling compares actual results against a financial forecast (cost and revenue estimates), using sales analysis, market share analysis and marketing profitability analysis, then revises the strategy — through changing the marketing mix, new product development or product deletion. Real example: Canva's marketing plan is visible end-to-end in its freemium model — around 220 million monthly active users (December 2024) and only about 21 million paying subscribers (September 2024), a conversion rate near 11% that functions as the core marketing objective the business monitors and controls toward, rather than reach alone.

groups.title: Marketing strategies
points: Market segmentation divides the total market into groups sharing common characteristics, letting a business tailor its marketing mix to a chosen segment for a competitive advantage, e.g. Qantas using behavioural segmentation to run Jetstar for price-sensitive leisure travellers alongside Qantas for business travellers.
Product/service differentiation develops and promotes differences from competitors, based on quality, value, convenience, customer service, or social/ethical/environmental considerations.

Positioning is creating an image or identity for a product relative to competitors' — e.g. Zara repositioning itself as a premium brand through logo and advertising changes in 2019. Real example: Kmart's own-brand Anko does two jobs at once — it lowers cost of goods sold and functions as the positioning statement, letting Kmart hold price leadership without needing to discount.

Product strategy covers branding (a name, term, symbol or design that identifies and differentiates a product — manufacturer, private/house or generic brands) and packaging (protection, attention, convenience) and labelling.

Pricing methods set the base price: cost-based (cost plus a margin), market-based (what the market will pay, given supply and demand) and competition-based (set relative to competitors' prices). Pricing strategies then adjust it: price skimming (highest possible price at launch, e.g. Apple), price penetration (lowest possible price to gain market share fast), loss leaders (sold at or below cost to draw customers into a store) and price points (psychological pricing, e.g. $19.95 vs $20).

The promotion mix combines advertising (paid, non-personal, mass-audience), personal selling (direct, one-to-one, expensive but persuasive), relationship marketing (long-term loyalty programs, e.g. Qantas Frequent Flyer), sales promotions (discounts, competitions, free samples), and publicity/public relations (often free, but with less control over the message) — reinforced by opinion leaders and word of mouth. Real example: Canva grew to around 220 million monthly active users largely through product-led and word-of-mouth marketing rather than traditional advertising.

Place/distribution channels range from producer-to-consumer (no intermediaries) up to producer-agent-wholesaler-retailer-consumer; channel choice is intensive (saturate the market, e.g. milk), selective (moderate coverage, e.g. clothing) or exclusive (one outlet per region, e.g. luxury brands); physical distribution covers transport, warehousing and inventory.

Global marketing can use a standardised approach (same marketing mix everywhere — cheaper, consistent, e.g. aspects of Nike) or a customised approach (adapted to local tastes and culture — more expensive but more locally relevant, e.g. 7-Eleven in Japan); global pricing options include customised pricing, market-customised pricing and standard worldwide pricing. Real example: Canva is a 'born-global' service brand, reaching roughly US$3 billion in annualised revenue in 2025 with minimal need to localise its core product, while Kmart's Anko brand is being customised into new markets like the Philippines through local stores and wholesale partnerships — showing the standardisation/customisation choice depends heavily on whether the product is a digital service or a physical good.

Technology increasingly shapes marketing directly through e-marketing and the collection of customer data — but data practices carry regulatory and reputational risk if customers are not properly informed. Real example: Bunnings used facial recognition technology in stores from November 2018 to November 2021; the Privacy Commissioner found in November 2024 that this breached the Privacy Act, and while the Administrative Review Tribunal partly overturned the finding in February 2026, it upheld the transparency and notification failures — showing that even where data collection is ultimately excused, failing to tell customers is itself a reputational risk.

questions.questionHtml: Explain why goods and/or services are central to both marketing and operations.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Explain marketing's role in identifying what customers want.
  • Explain operations' role in producing it.
  • Link the two together with an example.
Sample answer

Goods and services are the core output both functions are organised around. Marketing identifies what customers need and want through market research, shaping which goods or services the business should offer and how they should be positioned, priced and promoted. Operations is then responsible for actually producing those goods or services to the standard and volume the market demands. For example, if marketing promotes a product as being available by a certain date, operations must plan its transformation process to make that possible. Without this interdependence, a business could market a product it can't actually produce, or produce goods nobody wants — both functions rely on each other to satisfy customers and achieve profit maximisation.

questions.questionHtml: Discuss why ethical behaviour and government regulation are both important in marketing.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Explain the purpose of consumer/competition law.
  • Explain why ethical behaviour goes further than the law.
  • Give an example of each.
Sample answer

Government regulation, such as the Australian Consumer Law (2011) and the Competition and Consumer Act 2010, protects consumers against unfair practices like deceptive advertising and price discrimination, and protects competition by banning cartel conduct and predatory pricing — enforced by the ACCC and ASIC, with penalties up to $1.1 million for companies. Without this regulation, businesses could mislead customers or restrict competition, reducing consumer choice and trust.

Ethical behaviour matters because it goes beyond what the law strictly requires — for example, avoiding exaggerated claims or harmful stereotypes in advertising, even where these aren't explicitly illegal. Ethical marketing builds long-term customer loyalty and a positive reputation, attracting more investors and talented employees, whereas unethical practices like sugging (disguising sales as market research) damage trust even when not illegal. Together, regulation sets the legal floor and ethics raises the standard businesses should aim for.

questions.questionHtml: Using a real example, examine how ethics and the law both shape a business's marketing decisions.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Name a real, dated case and the law it breached.
  • Explain the financial and reputational consequences.
  • Draw a conclusion about why regulation matters.
Sample answer

The ACCC took Qantas to court in August 2023 for advertising and selling tickets on flights it had already decided to cancel, and for failing to promptly notify more than 10,000 existing ticketholders — conduct that ran from 21 May 2021 to 26 August 2023 and breached the Australian Consumer Law's protections against misleading conduct. Qantas settled, agreeing to a $100 million penalty plus roughly $20 million in direct payments to 86,597 eligible consumers ($225 for domestic tickets, $450 for international).

This shows why government regulation matters: without the ACCC's intervention, Qantas had a financial incentive to keep selling seats on flights operations had already withdrawn. It also shows the interdependence between ethics and regulation — the conduct wasn't just illegal, it was a marketing promise (a confirmed flight) that operations could no longer deliver on, and the $120 million total cost demonstrates that unethical promotion carries a direct financial cost on top of the reputational damage of the case becoming public.

questions.questionHtml: Two Australian board game publishers sell into the same national market. Tablework Games designs intricate strategy titles, prints runs of 2,000 copies and sells them through 15 specialist hobby stores at $95 each. Party Deck prints general-audience card games by the truckload and sells them through every major supermarket and discount retailer nationally at $12 each. Using the stimulus, distinguish between a mass market and a niche market.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Define mass market and niche market.
  • Apply each to the correct business in the stimulus.
Sample answer

A mass market is a large, broad market in which a business sells an undifferentiated product to as many customers as possible, while a niche market is a small, specific segment with distinct needs that a business targets with a more specialised offering. Party Deck is targeting the mass market: its low $12 price point and distribution through every major supermarket and discount retailer nationally are designed to appeal to the broadest possible range of casual buyers. Tablework Games is targeting a niche market: intricate strategy titles, small print runs of 2,000 copies, distribution through only 15 specialist hobby stores and a premium $95 price point are all aimed at a narrower segment of customers who specifically value depth and design over convenience and low price.

questions.questionHtml: A furniture retailer advertised a leather sofa at 'was $3600, now $1800 — half price'. An ACCC investigation found the sofa had only ever been sold at $3600 for a six-day period two years earlier. Using the stimulus, explain how the law regulating deceptive and misleading advertising affects a business's marketing.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Explain what the law prohibits.
  • Apply it to the retailer's conduct.
  • Note the consequence of breach.
Sample answer

Australian Consumer Law prohibits businesses from engaging in conduct that is misleading or deceptive, or likely to mislead or deceive, including false claims about discounts and 'was' pricing. In this case, advertising the sofa as 'was $3600' implies that $3600 was its genuine, ongoing price, when it was in fact only offered at that price for six days two years earlier — meaning the advertised 'half price' saving was substantially overstated and likely to mislead customers into believing they were getting a better deal than they actually were. This constrains how a business can market discounts: any reference price used in a sale advertisement must reflect a price the product was genuinely, regularly sold at, not an inflated figure used only to make a discount look larger. Breaching this law exposes a business to ACCC action, including significant fines and reputational damage, so marketing departments must ensure promotional pricing claims can be substantiated before they are published.

questions.questionHtml: An energy drink containing high levels of caffeine and sugar is marketed with cartoon mascots and sponsors prizes at primary school fun runs. Using the stimulus, discuss the ethical issues in marketing products that may damage health.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Point for: the business's commercial right to market a legal product.
  • Point against: the vulnerability of the audience being targeted.
  • Reach a conclusion.
Sample answer

On one hand, the energy drink is a legal product and the business has a commercial right to promote it, and prize sponsorship can provide genuine funding that school events rely on. On the other hand, using cartoon mascots and targeting primary-school-aged children through fun runs is ethically concerning because young children are a particularly vulnerable audience who are less able to critically evaluate marketing messages or understand the health risks of a high-caffeine, high-sugar product — especially when a playful, child-friendly mascot implies the product is fun and harmless rather than something with real health consequences for young bodies. On balance, even though the marketing is legal, deliberately building brand familiarity in young children around a product not recommended for their age group raises a genuine ethical concern about exploiting a vulnerable audience for long-term commercial gain, and a business claiming to act responsibly should weigh this reputational and ethical risk against the marketing benefit of school-event sponsorship.

questions.questionHtml: Explain how a SWOT analysis and the product life cycle are both used in a business's situational analysis.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Define SWOT and give an example of each element.
  • Define the four product life cycle stages briefly.
  • Explain why both tools help a business understand its market position.
Sample answer

A SWOT analysis identifies a business's internal Strengths (e.g. strong brand reputation) and Weaknesses (e.g. out-of-date market research), which can be directly controlled, and external Opportunities (e.g. a growing customer base) and Threats (e.g. a competitor releasing a superior product), which can only be responded to. This helps a business decide which strategies suit its current position.

The product life cycle tracks a product through introduction (low sales, high promotional cost, low price to build awareness), growth (rising sales and profit as the brand becomes established), maturity (peak demand, market saturation, focus shifts to retaining customers) and decline (falling sales as customers move to newer products). Each stage needs a different marketing mix — for example, heavy promotion in introduction, and reduced promotion in decline. Together, SWOT and the product life cycle give a business a full picture of both its internal/external position and where its products sit over time, informing what marketing strategy to develop next.

questions.questionHtml: Compare primary and secondary market research data.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Define both types.
  • Compare cost/time/specificity.
  • Give an example source of each.
Sample answer

Primary data is collected from original sources specifically to solve a business's own marketing problem, using methods like surveys, focus groups or observation. It is more specific and useful to the exact problem, but takes more time and money to collect.

Secondary data has already been collected by someone else for a different purpose, such as Australian Bureau of Statistics census data or industry reports. It is cheaper and faster to access, but is less specific to the business's particular marketing question, since it wasn't designed to answer it. Most businesses use a combination of both, using cheaper secondary data to build a general picture before spending on primary research to answer the specific question at hand.

questions.questionHtml: Analyse the marketing plan of a real Australian business, referring to at least two elements of the marketing process.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Name the business and be specific about its marketing approach.
  • Cover at least two elements of the marketing process (situational analysis, market research, objectives, target market, strategy, implementation/monitoring).
  • Support with real, dated figures.
Sample answer

Canva's marketing plan can be read directly from its freemium business model. Its target market is identified through segmentation into free users, Canva Pro/Teams subscribers, and education/non-profit tiers — a deliberate strategy that uses the free tier as a customer acquisition channel rather than a giveaway. By December 2024 Canva reported around 220 million monthly active users, up from 200 million just two months earlier, showing rapid growth in reach.

Implementation, monitoring and controlling is visible in Canva's own reported metric: around 21 million paying subscribers as of September 2024, a freemium-to-paid conversion rate of roughly 11%. This is the marketing objective the business is really managing toward — not raw user numbers, but the rate at which free users convert to paying ones — and Canva's annualised revenue passing US$3 billion in 2025 (up from about US$2.4 billion in mid-2024) shows that objective being met. Canva's growth was driven largely by product-led and word-of-mouth promotion rather than traditional paid advertising, showing a marketing plan doesn't need every element of the promotion mix to be effective if the product itself drives referral.

questions.questionHtml: A kitchenware brand launched a reusable coffee cup four years ago. Sales climbed for the first eighteen months, held steady for a year, and have now dropped 22% as several competitors entered with cheaper versions of the same design. Using the stimulus, explain how the stage of the product life cycle influences this business's marketing strategy.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Identify the current life cycle stage.
  • Explain why the strategy should change at this stage.
Sample answer

The pattern described — strong early growth, a period holding steady, and now a 22% sales decline as lower-priced competitors enter — indicates the product has moved from the growth stage into decline, having passed through a maturity/saturation stage as competitors caught up. At the decline stage, a marketing strategy built around growth (broad promotion, expanding distribution) is no longer appropriate, since the market is now saturated with cheaper alternatives. The business needs to shift strategy: options include reducing promotional spend and letting the product wind down profitably while resources move to a new product, discounting price to remain competitive against the cheaper entrants, or attempting to reposition the product around a point of difference the lower-priced competitors don't offer. Continuing to market the coffee cup as if it were still in its growth stage would waste marketing spend on a product whose sales trajectory has now clearly turned downward.

questions.questionHtml: A sporting goods chain budgeted for $2.8 million in online sales this quarter but achieved only $1.9 million, while its physical stores outperformed their budget by 12%. Digital channels received 65% of the marketing budget. Using the stimulus, explain how this business would monitor and control its marketing plan.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Explain the role of comparing actual results to the financial forecast.
  • Apply the comparison to the online vs. store result.
  • Explain what revision might follow.
Sample answer

Monitoring and controlling a marketing plan involves regularly comparing actual results against the financial forecast set during planning, so that any gap between planned and actual performance can be identified and acted on. In this case, the comparison reveals a clear problem: online sales reached only $1.9 million against a $2.8 million target — a shortfall of roughly 32% — despite 65% of marketing spend being directed digitally, while store sales, which received a smaller share of the budget, exceeded their target by 12%. This tells the business its digital marketing spend is not converting into online sales as efficiently as expected, relative to how effectively its in-store efforts are performing. Based on this, the business should revise its marketing strategy — for example, investigating whether the digital campaigns are reaching the right target market or whether the online purchase experience itself is the barrier — rather than continuing to direct the majority of its budget toward a channel that is currently underperforming its forecast so significantly.

questions.questionHtml: Evaluate the marketing strategies a business could use for a good or service, using the 4 Ps.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Cover Product, Price, Promotion and Place.
  • Give at least one strategy option and its trade-off under each P.
  • Reach an overall judgement about which combination best suits the scenario given.
Sample answer

Product decisions should be based on what customers actually need and want, not just what's easiest to produce — this includes features, packaging, branding and warranties. Price is the only element of the marketing mix that directly generates revenue and is also the most flexible to adjust; a business must choose between cost-based, market-based or competition-based pricing methods, then apply a strategy like price skimming (high initial price to recover R&D costs, e.g. Apple) or price penetration (low initial price to build market share fast).

Promotion should combine multiple methods — advertising for reach, sales promotions to drive trial, and relationship marketing (like loyalty programs) to retain existing customers — since no single method reaches every customer segment. Place/distribution should match the product: a low-cost, high-volume good suits intensive distribution through many retailers, while a premium good may suit exclusive distribution through few, carefully chosen outlets.

Ultimately, all 4 Ps must be integrated and consistent with each other — a premium positioning strategy (high price, exclusive distribution) only works if promotion and product design also reinforce a premium image, so the marketing mix should be evaluated as a whole rather than element by element.

questions.questionHtml: Analyse a marketing plan for a business, focusing on market segmentation and positioning.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Define segmentation and positioning.
  • Use a real or hypothetical example to show how they connect.
Sample answer

Market segmentation divides the total market into groups sharing common characteristics, letting a business choose the segment (or segments) most attractive to target — for example, Qantas segments the travel market behaviourally by purpose of trip, running the discount airline Jetstar for price-sensitive leisure travellers while Qantas itself targets business travellers willing to pay more for service and international reach.

Positioning then shapes how the business wants each segment to perceive its product relative to competitors — Jetstar is positioned around low cost and no-frills convenience, while Qantas is positioned around premium service and a wider international network. This dual-brand strategy lets the business capture two very different segments without either brand's positioning undermining the other's, since customers clearly understand what each brand stands for. A marketing plan that segments the market clearly, and positions each product deliberately within its segment, is more likely to reach the right customers efficiently than a single one-size-fits-all approach.

questions.questionHtml: Explain how globalisation has affected marketing management, referring to standardisation and customisation.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Explain globalisation's general effect on marketing.
  • Define and contrast standardisation and customisation.
  • Support with an example of each.
Sample answer

Globalisation has given businesses access to far more potential customers, but has also meant they may need to adapt their marketing mix to suit different local tastes, cultures and regulations, while facing increased competition from businesses worldwide.

A standardised approach keeps the same marketing mix in every country, assuming customer needs are similar everywhere — this reduces costs since the product, branding and promotion don't need to be redeveloped for each market, and lets a business take advantage of economies of scale. Canva is a useful example of a 'born-global' service that needed relatively little localisation to reach an annualised revenue passing US$3 billion in 2025, since a design platform serves a broadly similar need everywhere.

A customised approach adapts the marketing mix to local social, cultural and economic differences — for example, Kmart's Anko own-brand is being taken offshore through stores in the Philippines and wholesale distribution partnerships with major overseas retailers, adapting how the brand reaches each new market rather than simply exporting the same Australian retail format. Customisation can grow sales and brand reputation by respecting local preferences, but costs more time and money than standardisation. Businesses often blend the two, standardising where possible and customising only where local differences genuinely require it.

questions.questionHtml: Using a real example, discuss the risks a business takes on when it collects customer data as part of its marketing strategy.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Explain why businesses collect customer data.
  • Use a real, dated example of a data practice going wrong.
  • Distinguish between the legality and the ethics of the practice.
Sample answer

Collecting customer data lets a business understand behaviour, personalise marketing and improve targeting — a legitimate and increasingly central part of e-marketing. However, how that data is collected and disclosed carries real legal and reputational risk.

Bunnings used facial recognition technology in stores from November 2018 to November 2021 to identify people involved in prior incidents, scanning every customer entering a participating store. The Privacy Commissioner found in November 2024 that this breached the Privacy Act, and while the Administrative Review Tribunal partly overturned the finding on appeal in February 2026, it upheld the failures around transparency and notifying customers the technology was in use.

This shows that even where a data practice is ultimately found (on appeal) to be legally permissible, failing to properly inform customers is still a reputational risk in its own right — a business's customers may object to a practice on principle even if a regulator eventually accepts it. Ethical marketing means being transparent about data collection before a regulator forces disclosure, not just staying inside the letter of the law.

questions.questionHtml: A headphone brand releases a new noise-cancelling model at $650 for the first four months, then drops it to $420. A rival releases a comparable model at $199 from day one to build its user base quickly. Using the stimulus, distinguish between price skimming and penetration pricing.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Define price skimming and apply it to the first business.
  • Define penetration pricing and apply it to the competitor.
Sample answer

Price skimming is a strategy of setting a high initial price to maximise revenue from customers most willing to pay before gradually lowering it, while penetration pricing is a strategy of setting a low initial price to build market share and sales volume quickly. The headphone brand releasing its model at $650 before dropping it to $420 after four months is using price skimming — capturing high margins from early adopters willing to pay a premium for the newest product, before lowering the price to attract more price-sensitive buyers once that segment is exhausted. The rival launching a comparable model at $199 from day one is instead using penetration pricing — accepting lower margins per unit in order to win market share and build a large user base quickly, which may also help it establish brand loyalty before raising prices later.

questions.questionHtml: A jewellery house sells its $14,000 signature collection through a single boutique in each state capital, while its $89 costume-jewellery line is stocked in department stores, pharmacies and airport gift shops nationwide. Using the stimulus, distinguish between intensive, selective and exclusive distribution.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Define all three distribution approaches.
  • Apply exclusive distribution to the $14,000 collection.
  • Apply intensive distribution to the $89 range.
Sample answer

Intensive distribution makes a product available through as many outlets as possible, selective distribution uses a limited number of outlets that meet certain criteria, and exclusive distribution uses only one or a very small number of outlets in a given area. The jewellery house's $14,000 signature collection is sold through exclusive distribution — a single boutique per state capital protects the product's premium image and lets the business maintain tight control over how it is presented and sold, which matters far more for a luxury item than wide availability does. The $89 costume-jewellery line, by contrast, is sold through intensive distribution — department stores, pharmacies and airport gift shops all stocking it maximises convenience and exposure for a lower-priced, higher-volume product where broad availability drives sales more than an exclusive image would.

questions.questionHtml: Northbound Outdoor is an Australian hiking-gear brand. In the past year it has ended its supply agreements with big-box retailers and moved to a direct-to-consumer website plus two flagship stores, raised prices by 18%, and shifted most of its promotion spend from catalogue advertising to outdoor-adventure content creators. Revenue is up 4%, gross margin is up 11 percentage points, and unit sales are down 14%. Using the stimulus, evaluate the marketing strategies used by Northbound Outdoor.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Assess the distribution strategy (moving to exclusive channels) against the data.
  • Assess the pricing and promotion changes against the data.
  • Reach a substantiated overall judgement.
Sample answer

Northbound Outdoor's shift to direct-to-consumer distribution — its own website and two flagship stores, dropping big-box retail agreements — appears to have been an effective repositioning move: it has allowed the brand tighter control over its image and pricing, consistent with the 11-percentage-point improvement in gross margin, since big-box supply agreements typically come with wholesale discounts and lower margins than direct-to-consumer sales. The 18% price rise, combined with the shift to adventure-content-creator promotion, appears to have successfully repositioned the brand as more premium — revenue is up 4% and margins have improved significantly, even though unit sales have fallen 14%, meaning the business is selling fewer items at a considerably higher margin per item. Overall, these strategies should be judged a success on the evidence given: the combination of direct distribution, higher pricing and margin-focused promotion has grown revenue and substantially improved profitability, even though it has meant a smaller, more premium customer base — the key limitation is that this data covers only one year, and it is not yet clear whether the 14% unit sales decline will stabilise or continue to worsen as the brand loses reach among customers who previously bought it through big-box retailers.

trivia.questionHtml: What are the 4 Ps of the marketing mix?
trivia.answerHtml: Product, Price, Promotion and Place.

trivia.questionHtml: What's the difference between the selling approach and the marketing approach?
trivia.answerHtml: The selling approach (1920s–60s) emphasised persuading customers to buy; the marketing approach (1960s–present) researches what customers want first, then satisfies it.

trivia.questionHtml: What is a niche market?
trivia.answerHtml: A narrow, specific market segment with unique needs, too small for large mass-market businesses to bother targeting.

trivia.questionHtml: What does the Australian Consumer Law (2011) do?
trivia.answerHtml: A single national law giving all Australian consumers the same rights and all businesses the same obligations.

trivia.questionHtml: What is price discrimination?
trivia.answerHtml: Charging different prices for the same product in different markets — illegal unless justified by cost differences or matching a competitor in good faith.

trivia.questionHtml: What is sugging?
trivia.answerHtml: A sales approach disguised as market research — not illegal, but raises ethical concerns about deception and privacy.

trivia.questionHtml: What does SWOT stand for?
trivia.answerHtml: Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats.

trivia.questionHtml: What are the four stages of the product life cycle?
trivia.answerHtml: Introduction, growth, maturity, decline.

trivia.questionHtml: What is primary market research data?
trivia.answerHtml: Data collected first-hand by/for a business to solve its own specific marketing problem, e.g. surveys.

trivia.questionHtml: What is secondary market research data?
trivia.answerHtml: Data already collected by someone else for another purpose, e.g. ABS census data.

trivia.questionHtml: What is market segmentation?
trivia.answerHtml: Dividing the total market into groups of customers who share common characteristics.

trivia.questionHtml: What is product/service positioning?
trivia.answerHtml: Creating an image or identity for a product in customers' minds, relative to competing products.

trivia.questionHtml: What is price skimming?
trivia.answerHtml: Charging the highest possible price during a product's introduction stage, e.g. Apple.

trivia.questionHtml: What is price penetration?
trivia.answerHtml: Setting the lowest possible price to quickly gain market share, then raising prices later.

trivia.questionHtml: What is a loss leader?
trivia.answerHtml: A product sold at or below cost to draw customers into a store, who then buy other, more profitable items.

trivia.questionHtml: What is relationship marketing?
trivia.answerHtml: Developing long-term, cost-effective relationships with individual customers, e.g. loyalty programs.

trivia.questionHtml: What's the difference between publicity and public relations?
trivia.answerHtml: Publicity is free, unpaid news coverage; public relations are planned activities (e.g. sponsorships) to build a favourable image.

trivia.questionHtml: What is intensive distribution?
trivia.answerHtml: Saturating the market by using as many outlets as possible, suited to convenience goods like milk.

trivia.questionHtml: What is exclusive distribution?
trivia.answerHtml: Using only one retail outlet per large geographic area, suited to premium/luxury products.

trivia.questionHtml: What is standardised global marketing?
trivia.answerHtml: Keeping the same marketing mix in every country a product is sold in.

trivia.questionHtml: What is customised global marketing?
trivia.answerHtml: Adapting the marketing mix to suit local tastes, culture and conditions in each market.

trivia.questionHtml: What are the four segmentation variables for consumer markets?
trivia.answerHtml: Demographic, geographic, psychographic and behavioural.

trivia.questionHtml: What did the Federal Court find about Coles' 'Down Down' promotions on 14 May 2026?
trivia.answerHtml: That 13 of 14 promotional tickets examined were misleading, because prices had been temporarily raised before being advertised as discounted, breaching the Australian Consumer Law.

trivia.questionHtml: How did Coles advertise Karicare formula as a 'Down Down' discount, according to the Federal Court case?
trivia.answerHtml: Held at $18 for 794 days, raised to $24 for 23 days, then advertised as 'Down Down' at $21 — still $3 above the original price.

trivia.questionHtml: What were Qantas' 'ghost flights', and what penalty did it agree to?
trivia.answerHtml: Advertising and selling tickets on already-cancelled flights, and not promptly notifying ticketholders — Qantas agreed to a $100 million penalty plus about $20 million in payments to 86,597 consumers.

trivia.questionHtml: What did the ACCC's supermarkets inquiry (final report, February 2025) find?
trivia.answerHtml: An oligopolistic market structure — Woolworths (~38%) and Coles (~29%) of grocery sales — with limited incentive to compete vigorously on price, leading to 20 recommendations.

trivia.questionHtml: What is 'shrinkflation', as referenced in the ACCC supermarkets inquiry?
trivia.answerHtml: Reducing a product's size or quantity while keeping the price the same (or increasing it) — the inquiry recommended businesses be required to disclose it.

trivia.questionHtml: What is Canva's freemium conversion rate, and what does it show about its marketing objective?
trivia.answerHtml: Around 11% (21 million paying subscribers out of ~220 million monthly active users) — showing the marketing objective is conversion, not just reach.

trivia.questionHtml: How did Canva grow its user base, according to the case study?
trivia.answerHtml: Largely through product-led and word-of-mouth marketing rather than traditional advertising.

trivia.questionHtml: What real example shows own-branding doing both a cost and a positioning job at once?
trivia.answerHtml: Kmart's Anko brand — it lowers cost of goods sold and is itself the positioning statement, letting Kmart hold price leadership without discounting.

trivia.questionHtml: What did the Privacy Commissioner find about Bunnings' facial recognition technology in November 2024?
trivia.answerHtml: That its use in stores from November 2018 to November 2021 breached the Privacy Act, particularly around transparency and notification.

trivia.questionHtml: What law does the ACCC primarily enforce in marketing regulation?
trivia.answerHtml: The Australian Consumer Law (Schedule 2 of the Competition and Consumer Act 2010).

trivia.questionHtml: What is greenwashing?
trivia.answerHtml: Making misleading or exaggerated claims about a product's or business's environmental or ethical credentials.
